These are not throttled Stockfish engines but Maia-3, a network trained on HUMAN games: it plays the moves that players of your level actually play, mistakes included. Each character adds a style — attack, trades, gambits — that COLOURS that distribution without replacing it: it never buys a blunder Maia judged unlikely.

136 courses, each split into chapters. The comments come from the positions themselves, and the percentages are those of club games. Endgames follow the same format as openings: they are positions to understand, not to memorise.

It is Maia\'s human scale, close to Lichess\'s. It is NOT comparable to a « Stockfish level »: a Stockfish throttled to 1100 beats a Maia set to 2200, because it calculates where the other recognises. Two scales, two different things.
Everything. No account, no network, no data leaving the device. The engine, the puzzles, the courses and the opponents are all embedded.

One try by default. Three invite you to try a move « just to see », exactly the opposite of what a puzzle trains: you calculate the line to the end BEFORE you touch the piece. The three-try net is still in the settings.

Maia does not calculate: it can miss a mate in two or spoil an elementary endgame. Above a certain level, Stockfish takes over in FOUR cases only — a mate in one or two, an endgame with few pieces, a repetition in a winning position, and the case where the model does not answer. Below that level, missing a mate is PART of the character.

The board is found automatically by its checkerboard pattern, and you adjust the four corners if needed. Piece recognition is automatic; the SIDE TO MOVE, the CASTLING RIGHTS and EN PASSANT cannot be read from an image, and the app does not invent them — correct them yourself.

Training plays a course on a single continuous board: you play YOUR side, the partner answers on the main line. Every position you play is graded on its own — a mistake means « again », a hint caps the grade at « hard » — and FSRS schedules when you see it again. The unit is the POSITION, never the line: a position learned in one opening counts in every opening it transposes to.

They are not played by the rules of classical chess but REFEREED by an engine that knows them: the position and the legal moves come from it. That is what makes Atomic or Antichess possible without rewriting seven sets of rules.

The points A has scored, as a percentage of the maximum: a win is worth 1 point, a draw ½, a loss 0.
50%% means the two settings are level. Everything else, the Elo difference included, is derived from it.

The results in detail, always from A’s point of view.
Draws count as half a win in the score, but the LOS ignores them: they say nothing about who is stronger.

The difference in strength between A and B, converted from the score into Elo points. Positive when A is ahead.
The “±” is the 95%% confidence margin: the true value has 19 chances in 20 of lying inside it. That margin narrows as games accumulate — and it, not the Elo figure itself, is what tells you whether the series has run long enough.

The probability that A really is stronger than B, rather than the observed gap being chance.
It is computed on decisive games only: draws do not enter. Below 95%% the series has not settled anything, however clear the Elo difference looks. At 50%% the two sides are indistinguishable.

The average length of the finished games, in full moves (one move = one White ply plus one Black ply).
Short games often go with clear wins; long ones with balanced positions or hard-fought endgames.

The same thing as “W · D · L”, seen as a bar: the green part is what A won, the grey the draws, the red what B won.
A very wide grey band means the two settings are too close to be told apart — or that the thinking time is too short for the difference to show.

A’s score recalculated after every game, not game by game: the curve therefore starts very high or very low, then settles.
The pale band around it is the 95%% confidence interval. As long as it straddles the 50%% line, the series has settled nothing. It is the narrowing of that band that tells you when to stop.

The number of games finished.
The statistics above are recomputed after each one: they are volatile at first and steady later.

Two squares are WALLED: d4 and e5. Nothing lands there, nothing is captured there, and sliding pieces stop at them — only knights jump over. In every other respect, the rules of classical chess.
Three walls, two of which change square on EVERY half-move — and never the same one stays. No foothold lasts longer than a move, and you never know which one will hold.
After EVERY move, you place the duck on an empty square: it blocks it for everyone, cannot be captured, and must move each turn. No check, no checkmate, no stalemate — you win by CAPTURING the king.

The rules are those of classical chess. In addition: every %1$d moves played, you earn a token. You never hold more than ONE, and you cannot spend it while in check. Spending it lets you play TWO moves in a row — unless the first one checks your opponent, in which case the turn stops there.
